title: "Technical Appendix: SBayesRC-Style Annotation Priors"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    number-sections: true

This appendix describes the SBayesRC-style annotation-dependent BayesR prior
available through

```r
stblr_csr_annot(
  ...,
  annotation_model = "annotation_probit_stick"
)
```

The core prior family is closely aligned with published SBayesRC: marker
effects follow a multi-normal mixture and marker-specific mixture probabilities
are determined by conditional probit stick-breaking regressions on annotations.

The exposed `stblr_csr_annot()` model is not an exact reproduction of the
published GCTB SBayesRC implementation. Its default component-multiplier grid
differs, and this route uses the `sblr` CSR sparse-LD likelihood.

::: {.callout-note title="Software-status basis"}
Statements on current `sblr` defaults, supported routes, numerical safeguards,
and failure behavior on this page are reported from maintained developer
contracts or qualification records. They remain pending verification against
dispatch and source in phase 2; this qualification does not make the
statistical definitions themselves provisional.
:::

The separate scalar

```r
stblr_block_eigen(method = "sbayesrc")
```

route follows the GCTB/SBayesRC eigenspace-likelihood strategy in `sblr`
cross-product units. According to the current maintained block-eigen contract,
retained SBayesR/SBayesRC fitting defaults to the block-specific `gctb_block`
residual policy, while the older global projected policy is retained explicitly
as `global_projected_legacy`. Matching the default block policy still does not
establish equality of every likelihood, prior, preprocessing, and numerical
contract.

This page focuses on the annotation-dependent **probability architecture**,
its coefficient hierarchy, and its diagnostics. The underlying likelihood
operators are documented separately.

Throughout the Methods documentation:

- $X$ denotes the genotype matrix;
- $A$ denotes the raw marker-by-annotation matrix;
- $\widetilde A^{(P)}$ denotes the processed annotation design used by the
  probability architecture;
- lowercase $v$ denotes scalar variance and uppercase $V$ covariance;
- $\Pr(\cdot)$ denotes a probability statement; and
- implementation names are written in backticks.

## Single-trait model

For marker $j$, let

$$
c_j\in\{0,\ldots,K\}
$$

identify one of $K+1$ BayesR mixture components.

Conditional on component $c_j=k$,

$$
b_j
\mid
c_j=k,v_b,\gamma
\sim
N(0,\gamma_kv_b).
$$

The theoretical component ladder

$$
\gamma
=
(\gamma_0,\ldots,\gamma_K)
$$

contains fixed relative variance multipliers, while $v_b$ is the global
active-effect variance scale.

The maintained model contract, pending source verification in phase 2,
requires

$$
\gamma_0=0,
\qquad
\gamma_k>0
\quad
\text{for }k=1,\ldots,K.
$$

The first component is therefore an exact null state:

$$
b_j=0
\qquad
\text{when }c_j=0.
$$

The remaining components represent increasingly diffuse active-effect
distributions when the supplied $\gamma_k$ values increase.

### R indexing crosswalk

Current R vectors use one-based positions:

- `mixture_var[1]` corresponds to theoretical $\gamma_0$;
- R position `k + 1` corresponds to theoretical component $k$.

This is only an indexing crosswalk. It does not imply a rename of current code
fields or native component labels.

## Multiple columns in an ST fitter are not the joint MT model

If multiple traits are supplied to the single-trait annotation fitter, the
mixture construction and annotation coefficients are fitted separately by
trait.

The resulting annotation architectures are trait specific rather than one
joint multi-trait architecture.

This is distinct from the theoretical joint MT-BayesRC/SBayesRC model. No
public MT-BayesRC, MT-SBayesRC, annotation-informed MT, MT CSR, or MT
block-eigen fitter currently implements that model.

The joint MT model samples complete marker states with shared cross-trait
covariance and the factorized

$$
P\times H
$$

probability architecture described in
[MT BayesRC/SBayesRC](mt_bayesrc_sbayesrc.qmd).

## Optional BayesS-style `maf_effect_s`

The package argument `maf_effect_s` corresponds to the BayesS-style MAF
architecture parameter $S$.

According to the maintained capability contract, pending source verification
in phase 2, CSR SBayesRC supports both:

- fixed global `maf_effect_s`; and
- sampled trait-specific `maf_effect_s` through Metropolis-Hastings on
  validated ST routes.

SBayesRC annotations and MAF-S affect different parts of the prior:

- annotations affect marker-specific **component probabilities** through the
  probit-stick $P$ architecture;
- MAF-S affects marker-specific **effect variance** through a $Q$-type
  multiplier.

Let $f_j$ denote minor allele frequency and define heterozygosity

$$
h_j
=
2f_j(1-f_j).
$$

For standardized-genotype-scale effects, the current MAF-dependent prior
multiplier is

$$
q_j(S)
=
h_j^{S+1}.
$$

The $+1$ exponent reflects the standardized-genotype effect scale used by the
current summary-statistics parameterization.

For fixed $S$, a positive SBayesRC component has prior

$$
b_j
\mid
c_j=k>0,v_b,S
\sim
N\left(
0,
v_b\gamma_kq_j(S)
\right).
$$

Thus the full non-null variance is

$$
v_b\gamma_kq_j(S).
$$

Here $v_b$ is the global active-effect scale, $\gamma_k$ the BayesR component
multiplier, and $q_j(S)$ the MAF-S marker multiplier.

### Sampled $S$

When `maf_effect_s` is sampled, the maintained sampler contract reports one
$S_t$ per trait and chain, pending source verification in phase 2, using the
active-component log-posterior contribution

```text
log p(S_t | b_t, gamma_t, vb_t)
  = log p(S_t)
    - 0.5 sum_{j: gamma_jt > 0} [
        log q_j(S_t) + b_jt^2 / (vb_t gamma_jt q_j(S_t))
      ]
```

The same contract reports the sampled-$S$ defaults

```r
maf_effect_s_init = 0
maf_effect_s_prior = c(-3, 2)
maf_effect_s_proposal_sd = 0.35
```

Fixed `maf_effect_s` is available only where the public capability contract
marks it supported. Sampled `maf_effect_s` remains an ST-only capability on
validated routes.

See [`maf_effect_s`](../notes/maf_effect_s.qmd) and the current developer
capability documentation for route-specific support.

## Component-multiplier grids

According to the current maintained model contract, the public `sblr` default
is

```r
mixture_var = c(0, 0.01, 0.1, 1)
```

The published SBayesRC specification instead names five biological effect-size
classes---zero, very small, small, medium, and large---with component variances
expressed as percentages of total SNP genetic variance:

$$
\left(
0,
0.001\%,
0.01\%,
0.1\%,
1\%
\right)v_g^{\mathrm{SNP}}
=
\left(
0,
10^{-5},
10^{-4},
10^{-3},
10^{-2}
\right)v_g^{\mathrm{SNP}}.
$$

In the generic `sblr` parameterization $\gamma_kv_b$, the common factor
$10^{-2}v_g^{\mathrm{SNP}}$ can be absorbed into $v_b$. The corresponding
*relative* ladder is then

```r
mixture_var = c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1)
```

The same contract reports that the relative ladder can be requested explicitly:

```r
fit <- stblr_csr_annot(
  stats = stats,
  Glist = Glist,
  annotations = A,
  annotation_model = "annotation_probit_stick",
  mixture_var = c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1)
)
```

Matching this multiplier vector aligns the component ratios and restores the
published five-class ordering. It does not by itself align the absolute scale:
that also requires $v_b$ to have the corresponding interpretation. Nor does it
make the complete `sblr` model identical to GCTB SBayesRC, because likelihood,
residual-variance, preprocessing, hyperprior, and numerical contracts can still
differ.

## Raw and processed annotation designs

Let

$$
A\in\mathbb R^{M\times C}
$$

denote the raw marker-by-annotation matrix, where $M$ is the number of markers
and $C$ the number of annotation columns before or after any explicit intercept
handling.

The SBayesRC probability model acts on a processed design, denoted

$$
\widetilde A^{(P)}.
$$

This notation is useful because the preprocessing appropriate to a probability
architecture need not be identical to the preprocessing used by another prior
mechanism such as log-variance LV.

Rows must be aligned with the markers in:

- the sufficient statistics;
- the fitted LD/operator representation; and
- posterior marker summaries.

Columns may contain binary or quantitative annotations, and annotations may
overlap.

### Contract-reported preprocessing controls

According to the maintained annotation-preparation contract, pending source
verification in phase 2, the SBayesRC-style route uses controls including:

- `add_intercept = TRUE`, which adds an all-ones first column when an intercept
  is not already recognized;
- `standardize_annotations = TRUE`, which centers and scales eligible
  nonbinary quantitative annotations;
- `center_binary_annotations = FALSE`, which leaves binary annotation columns
  unchanged by default;
- marker names, when available, which may be used to reorder annotation rows to
  the declared analysis-marker order.

The preprocessing choices determine the meaning and scale of the fitted
annotation coefficients.

Under the defaults:

- a quantitative coefficient is interpreted per standardized annotation unit;
- an unchanged binary coefficient compares annotation membership conditional
  on the other annotation columns and on the stick position.

The processed design, rather than the raw $A$ itself, is the object entering
the mathematical linear predictor.

## Annotation-dependent component probabilities

For $K+1$ BayesR components, including the exact null component, there are $K$
conditional continuation steps.

Let

$$
\alpha_k
\in
\mathbb R^C
$$

be the coefficient vector for continuation step $k$, and define

$$
\eta_{jk}
=
\widetilde A_j^{(P)}\alpha_k.
$$

The conditional continuation probability is

$$
\rho_{jk}
=
\Phi(\eta_{jk}),
$$

where $\Phi$ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function.

The marker-specific prior component probabilities are

$$
P_{j0}
=
1-\rho_{j1},
$$

$$
P_{j1}
=
\rho_{j1}(1-\rho_{j2}),
$$

and more generally

$$
P_{jk}
=
\left(
\prod_{\ell=1}^{k}
\rho_{j\ell}
\right)
(1-\rho_{j,k+1}),
\qquad
k=1,\ldots,K-1,
$$

with final component probability

$$
P_{jK}
=
\prod_{\ell=1}^{K}
\rho_{j\ell}.
$$

Thus,

$$
\Pr(c_j=k\mid A_j)
=
P_{jk}.
$$

The annotation architecture therefore changes the prior probability that a
marker occupies each BayesR component. It does not directly change $v_b$ or the
component multipliers $\gamma_k$.

### Why the probabilities sum to one

For one marker, write its continuation probabilities as

$$
\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_K.
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=0}^{K}P_k
&=
(1-\rho_1)
+
\rho_1(1-\rho_2)
+
\cdots\\
&\quad+
\left(
\prod_{\ell=1}^{K-1}\rho_\ell
\right)
(1-\rho_K)
+
\prod_{\ell=1}^{K}\rho_\ell\\
&=
1.
\end{aligned}
$$

The expression telescopes: a marker either stops at one of the first $K$
continuation steps or reaches the final component.

## Numerical flooring and renormalization

According to the maintained sampler contract, pending source verification in
phase 2, the sampler computes component probabilities from the processed
annotation linear predictors, floors each probability at `pi_floor`, and
renormalizes each marker row to sum to one.

The contract-reported public default is

```r
pi_floor = 1e-12
```

Flooring prevents exact numerical zero probabilities when probit predictors are
extreme.

Because flooring slightly changes the unnormalized stick probabilities, the
subsequent row renormalization is required.

This is a numerical-stability adjustment, not a different conceptual link
function.

The deterministic R diagnostic helpers apply the mathematical stick-breaking
transform without the native sampler's floor-and-renormalize step. For ordinary
finite coefficients, their rows sum to one up to numerical tolerance.

## Intercept prior

At continuation step $k$, let $\alpha_{0k}$ denote the intercept coefficient.

According to the current maintained intercept qualification record, pending
source verification in phase 2, the standard contract uses the proper prior

$$
\alpha_{0k}
\sim
N(\mu_{0k},\tau_{0k}^2).
$$

By default,

$$
\mu_{0k}
=
\Phi^{-1}(\rho_k^{(0)}),
$$

where $\rho_k^{(0)}$ is the continuation probability implied by the resolved
global component mixture, and

$$
\tau_{0k}=1.
$$

`annotation_intercept_prior` can provide finite scalar or step-specific means
and standard deviations.

This prior specification is distinct from `alpha_init`, which controls only the
initial MCMC state.

The same qualification record reports that the historical flat-intercept mode
is available only through explicit

```r
intercept_flat = TRUE
```

and is retained as a legacy reference mode. Empty or completely separated
sticks do not define a proper flat-intercept posterior target. The reported
software behavior is to fail rather than silently continue under such a state;
that behavior awaits phase-2 source verification.

The published SBayesRC annotation regression used a flat intercept convention.
The proper default above is therefore a deliberate `sblr` model generalization,
not an exact reproduction of that part of the published prior.

## Non-intercept $\alpha$ hierarchy and `sigmaSqAlpha`

For non-intercept annotation coefficient $c$ at continuation step $k$, the
implemented prior is

$$
\alpha_{ck}
\mid
\sigma_{\alpha,k}^2
\sim
N(0,\sigma_{\alpha,k}^2).
$$

Each continuation step has its own annotation-effect variance

$$
\sigma_{\alpha,k}^2,
$$

represented in current code by `sigmaSqAlpha[k]`.

The intercept is excluded from this hierarchical shrinkage variance because it
has the separate prior above.

A scaled-inverse-chi-squared prior parameterized by degrees of freedom
$\nu_\alpha$ and scale $\tau_\alpha^2$ can be written

$$
\sigma_{\alpha,k}^2
=
\frac{\nu_\alpha\tau_\alpha^2}{\chi^2_{\nu_\alpha}}.
$$

After conditioning on the coefficients in $\mathcal R$, its conjugate update is

$$
\sigma_{\alpha,k}^2
=
\frac{
\sum_{c\in\mathcal R}\alpha_{ck}^2+b_\alpha
}{
\chi^2_{|\mathcal R|+a_\alpha}
},
$$

where $\mathcal R$ is the set of coefficients subject to hierarchical
shrinkage, with the parameter crosswalk

$$
a_\alpha=\nu_\alpha,
\qquad
b_\alpha=\nu_\alpha\tau_\alpha^2.
$$

According to the current maintained qualification record, the implementation
controls these hyperparameters through:

- `sigmaSqAlpha_a`, supplying $a_\alpha$;
- `sigmaSqAlpha_b`, supplying $b_\alpha$;
- `sigmaSqAlpha_init`, supplying the initial state.

That record reports current public defaults

$$
(a_\alpha,b_\alpha)=(2,2).
$$

The published specification used
$\nu_\alpha=4$ and $\tau_\alpha^2=1$. Under the convention displayed above,

$$
(a_\alpha,b_\alpha)
=
(4,4).
$$

The reported current defaults $(2,2)$ are therefore different from the
published hyperparameters. The two priors share a broad
scaled-inverse-chi-squared family but are not exactly equivalent.

For reproducibility, report the actual values used for:

- `sigmaSqAlpha_a`;
- `sigmaSqAlpha_b`;
- `sigmaSqAlpha_init`;
- `annotation_intercept_prior`; and
- `intercept_flat`, if legacy flat-intercept mode was explicitly requested.

## Gibbs-style $\alpha$ updating

According to the maintained sampler contract, pending source verification in
phase 2, when

```r
updateAlpha = TRUE
```

the sampler updates the annotation coefficients every `alpha_update_every`
iterations.

The contract-reported public default interval is 10.

The update uses conditional probit data augmentation.

### Eligible markers at one stick

At continuation step $k$, only markers that **reach that step** contribute to
the corresponding probit likelihood.

For each eligible marker $j$, introduce a latent normal variable

$$
\ell_{jk}
\mid
\alpha_k
\sim
N\left(
\widetilde A_j^{(P)}\alpha_k,
1
\right).
$$

The latent variable is truncated:

- above zero when the marker continues beyond step $k$;
- at or below zero when it stops at step $k$.

Thus the sign of the latent variable records the continuation outcome for that
stick.

### Coefficient update

Conditional on the latent variables and the other coefficients, each
annotation coefficient has a Gaussian full conditional.

For a non-intercept coefficient, the prior precision

$$
\frac{1}{\sigma_{\alpha,k}^2}
$$

is added to the data precision.

For the intercept, the proper-prior contribution is

$$
\frac{1}{\tau_{0k}^2}
$$

to the precision and

$$
\frac{\mu_{0k}}{\tau_{0k}^2}
$$

to the conditional right-hand side.

After the coefficients for a step are updated, `sigmaSqAlpha[k]` is drawn from
its hierarchical conditional update.

### Empty sticks

If no marker reaches a continuation step, there is no latent-data likelihood
for that stick.

Under the proper-intercept contract, the sampler then:

1. draws the intercept from its proper prior;
2. draws non-intercept coefficients from their hierarchical conditional prior;
3. performs the ordinary `sigmaSqAlpha` conditional update.

The sampler therefore has an explicit no-data behavior rather than relying on
an undefined regression fit.

### Nature of the update

The $\alpha$ update is a Gibbs-style conditional update based on:

- truncated-normal latent-variable draws; and
- Gaussian coefficient full conditionals.

It is **not** a random-walk Metropolis-Hastings update.

After an $\alpha$ update, the marker-specific prior component probabilities
$P_{jk}$ are recomputed from the updated processed annotation predictors.

## Initialization

According to the maintained initialization contract, pending source
verification in phase 2, `make_sbayesrc_alpha_init()` constructs deterministic
initial values for the annotation-dependent mixture architecture.

Given an initial overall active probability `pi_init`, it distributes active
probability mass across the $K$ non-null components using normalized
`active_comp_weights`.

This produces initial marginal component probabilities

$$
\pi^{(0)}
=
\left(
1-\pi_{\mathrm{init}},
\pi_{\mathrm{init}}w_1,
\ldots,
\pi_{\mathrm{init}}w_K
\right).
$$

The helper then converts those marginal probabilities into conditional
continuation probabilities.

If the processed annotation design contains an all-ones intercept column, the
intercept receives initial coefficients

$$
\alpha_{0k}^{(0)}
=
\Phi^{-1}
\left(
\rho_k^{(0)}
\right),
$$

and the remaining annotation coefficients begin at zero.

If no all-ones column is present, the default coefficient matrix begins at
zero.

Explicit `alpha_init` and `sigmaSqAlpha_init` values are accepted after
dimension and finite-value validation.

The helper also returns auditable quantities such as:

- initial component probabilities;
- normalized active-component weights;
- conditional continuation probabilities;
- component multipliers $\gamma$;
- component names.

Initialization is an MCMC starting-state choice. It is distinct from the
coefficient prior.

## Marker-effect and component updates

For each marker, the sampler combines:

1. the annotation-derived prior component probabilities $P_{jk}$; and
2. the marker-specific likelihood evidence.

The exact null component has

$$
\gamma_0=0
$$

and therefore fixes the marker effect to zero.

For active component $k>0$, without additional MAF-S scaling the prior variance
is

$$
v_{b,jk}
=
\gamma_kv_b.
$$

With MAF-S,

$$
v_{b,jk}
=
\gamma_kq_j(S)v_b.
$$

The sampler forms component-specific posterior weights from:

- the current marker score;
- residual variance $v_e$;
- the marker diagonal cross-product;
- the component prior variance; and
- the annotation-derived prior probability $P_{jk}$.

It then samples a new component and, if that component is positive, samples the
marker effect from its conditional Gaussian distribution.

When `updateB = TRUE`, the global scale $v_b$ can also be updated using the
currently active marker effects together with their selected component
multipliers.

Thus:

- $P_{jk}$ controls **which component is likely**;
- $\gamma_k$ controls the component's **relative effect-variance scale**;
- $v_b$ supplies the **global effect-variance scale**;
- $q_j(S)$, when enabled, supplies an additional marker-specific
  **variance multiplier**.

## Posterior architecture and marker quantities

The posterior mean coefficient matrix has annotation coefficients in rows and
continuation steps in columns. Because the stick transformation is nonlinear,

$$
\operatorname{stick}
\left(
\mathbb E(\alpha\mid\mathcal D)
\right)
$$

is generally not equal to

$$
\mathbb E
\left[
\operatorname{stick}(\alpha)
\mid
\mathcal D
\right].
$$

Applying the nonlinear stick transform to posterior mean $\alpha$ therefore
produces a plug-in diagnostic, not the posterior mean of the transformed prior
architecture. Posterior summaries of $\sigma_{\alpha,k}^2$ describe the
step-specific dispersion allowed among non-intercept annotation coefficients.

They should be interpreted together with:

- annotation preprocessing;
- $\alpha$ coefficients;
- component occupancy;
- chain diagnostics.

The marker-by-component posterior allocation probabilities record posterior
frequencies of component assignments after burn-in and thinning. They are
**not** the annotation-derived prior matrix

$$
P_{jk}
=
\Pr(c_j=k\mid A_j,\alpha).
$$

For marker $j$,

$$
\Pr(c_j=k\mid\mathcal D)
$$

is a posterior allocation probability and contains both prior and likelihood
information.

The mathematical ordering fixes component $k=0$ as null. Therefore the marker
PIP is

$$
\operatorname{PIP}_j
=
1-
\Pr(c_j=0\mid\mathcal D).
$$

Final sampled component states, posterior allocation probabilities, prior
component probabilities, and posterior mean effects should not be interpreted
interchangeably.

## Deterministic diagnostic helpers

The package exposes deterministic helpers that map fitted $\alpha$ values to
compact prior-architecture summaries.

These are useful diagnostics, but when supplied with posterior mean
coefficients they are plug-in summaries rather than full posterior
transformations.

### Annotation-row diagnostics

`sbayesrc_annotation_pi(alpha, gamma)` applies the probit stick-breaking
transform separately to each coefficient row in the representation expected by
the helper.

It returns an annotation-by-component probability matrix.

`sbayesrc_annotation_gamma_mean(alpha, gamma)` calculates the corresponding
expected component multiplier for an annotation-row diagnostic:

$$
\overline\gamma_c^{(\mathrm{annotation})}
=
\sum_{k=0}^{K}
\pi_{ck}\gamma_k.
$$

These are **coefficient-row diagnostics**.

For example, evaluating a binary annotation as a standalone row does not
automatically include:

- the fitted intercept;
- correlated annotations;
- the complete annotation profile of an actual marker.

The result should therefore not be described as the literal prior component
probability of every marker carrying that annotation.

### Marker-profile diagnostics

`sbayesrc_marker_pi(A, alpha, gamma)` first forms the annotation linear
predictors for complete marker profiles and then applies the stick-breaking
transform.

It returns an $M\times(K+1)$ marker-level prior component-probability matrix.

`sbayesrc_marker_gamma_mean(A, alpha, gamma)` calculates

$$
\overline\gamma_j^{(\mathrm{marker})}
=
\sum_{k=0}^{K}
P_{jk}\gamma_k.
$$

This expected multiplier is a one-number summary of the marker's complete prior
component distribution.

Marker-profile diagnostics are generally more directly connected to the fitted
prior architecture than standalone annotation-row diagnostics because they use
the complete marker annotation profile.

## Interpreting annotation effects

An $\alpha$ coefficient acts on one **conditional continuation probability**.

Its sign cannot be interpreted independently of the stick position.

At step $k$:

- a positive coefficient increases the probability of continuing beyond that
  stick;
- a negative coefficient increases the probability of stopping at that stick;
- its effect on the final component distribution depends on earlier and later
  continuation probabilities.

Therefore a raw coefficient is not a simple component-specific log-odds ratio.

### Expected component multiplier

The quantity

$$
\mathbb E_\text{prior}(\gamma_j)
=
\sum_{k=0}^{K}
P_{jk}\gamma_k
$$

is a useful scalar summary of prior mixture allocation.

However, it compresses a full component-probability vector.

Two markers can have the same expected multiplier while placing prior mass on
different BayesR components.

When component identity matters, report the full $P_{jk}$ vector rather than
only the expected multiplier.

### Prior architecture versus posterior marker evidence

A marker's prior component vector

$$
(P_{j0},\ldots,P_{jK})
$$

should be distinguished from its posterior component vector

$$
\left\{
\Pr(c_j=k\mid\mathcal D)
\right\}_{k=0}^{K}.
$$

The difference between the two reflects the contribution of the marker
likelihood and the rest of the hierarchical posterior.

Correlations between expected prior multiplier and posterior PIP can describe a
prior-posterior relationship, but they are not calibration statistics or
causal estimates.

## Convergence diagnostics should follow the hierarchy

Because the annotation model is hierarchical, convergence should be assessed at
more than one level.

A useful hierarchy is:

1. **raw coefficient state:** $\alpha$, `sigmaSqAlpha`, and their
   $\widehat R$, ESS, MCSE, and trace diagnostics;
2. **induced prior architecture:** marker-level $P_{jk}$, prior active
   probabilities, expected component multipliers, and expected occupancy;
3. **posterior marker inference:** posterior component probabilities, PIPs, and
   marker effects;
4. **downstream summaries:** variance components and prediction.

Good-looking coefficient means do not by themselves establish that the induced
marker prior is stable.

Conversely, uncertainty in raw coefficients can sometimes be partially
attenuated in downstream quantities.

For this reason, SBayesRC-style diagnostics should include both coefficient
space and induced marker-prior space.

## Comparison with published SBayesRC

The primary external reference for this comparison is
[Zheng et al. (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41588-024-01704-y).

The `sblr` column reports maintained-contract behavior pending phase-2 source
verification.

| Published SBayesRC feature | `sblr` implementation | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| BayesR-like multi-normal marker-effect mixture | $b_j\mid c_j=k\sim N(0,\gamma_kv_b)$ | Same core prior family |
| Exact null component | Requires first multiplier to be zero; null effects are exactly zero | Same |
| Five absolute classes $(0,0.001\%,0.01\%,0.1\%,1\%)v_g^{\mathrm{SNP}}$ | Supports the relative ladder `c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1)` with a separate $v_b$ | Same component ratios only when requested; absolute scale also depends on $v_b$ |
| Exposed default multiplier grid | `c(0, 0.01, 0.1, 1)` | Different default |
| Marker-specific component probabilities from annotations | Uses processed annotation predictors for every marker | Same core structure |
| Conditional probit stick breaking | Uses $\rho_{jk}=\Phi(\widetilde A_j^{(P)}\alpha_k)$ | Same core structure |
| Flat annotation-regression intercept | Proper mixture-calibrated normal intercept prior by default; flat only in explicit legacy mode | Deliberate model difference |
| Functional annotations | Accepts overlapping binary or quantitative annotations and adds an intercept by default | Closely aligned, with `sblr` preprocessing defaults |
| Quantitative annotation handling | Standardizes eligible nonbinary annotations by default; leaves binary columns unchanged by default | Qualified implementation choice |
| Normal non-intercept $\alpha$ prior with step-specific variance | $\alpha_{ck}\mid\sigma_{\alpha,k}^2\sim N(0,\sigma_{\alpha,k}^2)$ | Same broad prior family |
| Scaled inverse-chi-square annotation-variance prior with $\nu_\alpha=4$, $\tau_\alpha^2=1$ | Uses $(a_\alpha,b_\alpha)=(2,2)$ by reported default rather than the mapped published values $(4,4)$ | Same broad family, different hyperparameters |
| Probit coefficient update | Truncated-normal augmentation and conditional Gaussian draws | Closely aligned Gibbs-style update |
| Numerical component-probability handling | Floors probabilities at `pi_floor` and renormalizes | `sblr` numerical-stability detail |
| Summary-statistics likelihood | CSR sparse LD for `stblr_csr_annot()`; retained eigenspace for scalar `stblr_block_eigen()` | CSR is a different operator; retained fitting defaults to the block-specific compatibility policy but is not thereby identical in every contract |

The most accurate description is:

> `stblr_csr_annot(..., annotation_model = "annotation_probit_stick")`
> implements an SBayesRC-style annotation-dependent BayesR probability prior
> that is closely aligned with the published SBayesRC prior structure and is
> fitted using the `sblr` CSR sparse-LD likelihood.

It should not be described as an exact reproduction of the published GCTB
SBayesRC implementation under default `sblr` settings.

## Practical validation checklist

Before interpreting an SBayesRC-style fit:

1. verify marker alignment among annotations, sufficient statistics, the fitted
   LD/operator representation, and posterior marker summaries;
2. record the component-multiplier grid and distinguish the `sblr` default from
   the published grid;
3. record intercept handling, quantitative standardization, and binary
   centering;
4. inspect annotation prevalence, scale, overlap, and collinearity;
5. report `annotation_intercept_prior`, `sigmaSqAlpha_a`,
   `sigmaSqAlpha_b`, `pi_floor`, and `alpha_update_every`;
6. report whether legacy `intercept_flat = TRUE` was explicitly used;
7. inspect $\alpha$ and `sigmaSqAlpha` convergence;
8. inspect induced marker-level prior probabilities and expected occupancy;
9. inspect posterior component probabilities, PIPs, variance traces, and marker
   effects;
10. distinguish annotation-derived prior probabilities from posterior component
    frequencies;
11. compare standalone annotation-row diagnostics with full marker-profile
    diagnostics where useful;
12. assess sensitivity to the $\gamma$ grid, LD representation, annotations,
    preprocessing, and hyperparameters;
13. avoid causal interpretation of raw $\alpha$ coefficients or expected
    component multipliers.

## Joint MT factorization

For genuine joint MT BayesRC/SBayesRC, let

$$
P_{j0}
$$

be marker $j$'s null component probability and

$$
P_{jk},
\qquad
k>0,
$$

its positive-component probabilities.

Let

$$
H_p
$$

be the global conditional probability of non-null trait pattern $p$.

The current prior is

$$
\Pr(c_j=0\mid A_j)
=
P_{j0},
$$

and for $k>0$,

$$
\Pr(a_j=p,c_j=k\mid A_j)
=
P_{jk}H_p.
$$

The same probit-stick architecture governs $P$.

The sharing architecture $H$ is global and annotation independent.

Let

$$
\beta_j
=
B_{j\cdot}^{\top}
$$

denote the joint MT marker-effect vector.

Conditional on active pattern $p$ and positive component $k$,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(\beta_{j,p,k})
=
\gamma_kq_jV_{b,p},
$$

where $V_{b,p}$ is the active-trait submatrix of the global marker-effect
covariance $V_b$.

In the deferred MT-SBayesRC design, annotations modify $P$ but do not make $H$
or $V_b$ annotation dependent. No public MT-SBayesRC route currently implements
this design.

See [MT BayesRC/SBayesRC](mt_bayesrc_sbayesrc.qmd) for the complete joint MT
state model and output semantics.
